qs.q: A patient presents with signs of thyrotoxicosis and a large retrosternal goitre resulting in obstruction of the superior vena cava. What specific physical sign is classically associated with this superior vena cava obstruction?
qs.e: Pemberton's sign involves facial congestion and cyanosis upon raising both arms, indicating superior vena cava obstruction from a retrosternal goitre. Trousseau's and Chvostek's signs are tests for hypocalcemia.

exam: What bedside signs differentiate SVCO from simple facial oedema? — Look for distended neck veins, chest‑wall collaterals, and positional worsening.
A patient with HIV presents with mediastinal widening on X‑ray. What is your next diagnostic step? — Obtain CT chest to distinguish TB lymphadenitis from lymphoma.

How would you manage a patient with SVCO caused by a central‑line thrombosis when anticoagulation is contraindicated? — Consider catheter removal, mechanical thrombectomy if available, and urgent referral for stenting.
Why is single‑fraction radiotherapy preferred in an emergency SVCO? — It provides rapid tumour shrinkage, relieving obstruction within 24‑48 h.
What red‑flag symptom mandates immediate airway protection? — Stridor or progressive dyspnoea indicating laryngeal oedema.
Explain why a normal chest X‑ray does not exclude SVCO. — Early obstruction may not produce a visible mass; clinical signs guide further imaging.
In a low‑resource setting without CT, how can you confirm TB as the cause of SVCO? — Combine chest X‑ray, positive sputum/IGRA, and response to anti‑TB therapy.
What is the rationale for head‑of‑bed elevation in SVCO? — It reduces hydrostatic pressure in the upper veins, decreasing facial and neck swelling.
ai.title: Superior Vena Cava Obstruction
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Obstruction of the superior vena cava causes venous congestion of the head, neck and upper chest. Prompt recognition, identification of the underlying cause and relief of the obstruction are essential, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by imaging that shows a narrowed SVC or collateral veins.
sections.p: Partial or complete blockage of the superior vena cava impairs venous return from the face, neck, upper limbs and upper thorax, producing characteristic swelling and dilated chest‑wall veins.

t.b: Is there a mediastinal mass or widened mediastinum? → Suggests tumour, TB or lymphoma; if normal, consider thrombosis.
What is the cause and extent of obstruction? → Defines tumour, lymphadenopathy, thrombus, and collateral pathways.
Are neck veins compressible? → Non‑compressible suggests thrombosis when CT unavailable.

b: Mild: facial swelling only, no respiratory compromise.
Moderate: dyspnoea, cough, headache, visible chest‑wall collaterals.
Severe (life‑threatening): stridor, cerebral oedema, hypotension.
sections.p: Severity is graded by symptom burden and hemodynamic impact.

b: Bronchogenic carcinoma (especially small‑cell) – most frequent worldwide.
Mediastinal lymphoma (Hodgkin’s or non‑Hodgkin’s) – common in HIV‑positive patients.
Tuberculosis lymphadenitis or mediastinal TB mass – endemic.
Thrombosis of the SVC from central venous catheters or pacemaker leads.
Rare: metastatic breast or thyroid cancer, sarcoidosis, fungal infections.
sections.p: In low‑resource East African hospitals the most common aetiologies are infectious and malignant.

b: Facial plethora and periorbital oedema, worse in the morning.
Distended neck and chest‑wall veins, especially over the upper sternum.
Dyspnoea, cough, hoarseness, and a sensation of throat tightness.
Headache, visual disturbance, or confusion from cerebral venous congestion.
Upper‑limb swelling and venous engorgement.
sections.p: Patients develop a constellation of upper‑body venous congestion signs that progress from subtle to severe.
Select tests that answer the key clinical questions while considering resource limits.

t.b: Is there a mediastinal mass or pleural effusion? → Guides need for CT or urgent referral.
What is the exact cause and level of obstruction? → Determines need for radiotherapy, chemotherapy or surgery.
Is thrombosis present? → Indicates anticoagulation rather than oncologic therapy.
Is there evidence of infection, malignancy or immunosuppression? → Helps prioritize TB vs lymphoma.

t.b: Can we infer a mass or thrombus? → Proceed with empirical anti‑TB therapy or refer for urgent imaging.

b: Cerebral oedema → seizures, loss of consciousness.
Airway compromise from laryngeal oedema → stridor, respiratory arrest.
Superior vena cava thrombosis extending to brachiocephalic veins.
Concurrent mediastinal mass effects: spinal cord compression, pleural effusion.
sections.p: Complications arise from severe venous congestion and from the underlying disease.

b: If malignancy: start radiotherapy (single‑fraction 8 Gy if urgent) or chemotherapy for chemosensitive tumours.
If TB: initiate standard anti‑TB regimen (2 months intensive, 4 months continuation).
If thrombus: therapeutic anticoagulation (e.g., unfractionated heparin) unless contraindicated.
Supportive measures: elevate head of bed 30°, give supplemental O₂, treat cough with simple expectorants, use steroids only for airway oedema.
If no definitive therapy available, consider temporary endovascular stenting in referral centre.
sections.p: Treat the cause first, then relieve the obstruction and support the patient.

b: Re‑assess facial swelling and neck veins after 48 h of therapy.
Repeat chest X‑ray or ultrasound to ensure patency of SVC.
Educate patients with central lines on early signs of thrombosis.
Vaccinate HIV‑positive patients and screen for TB to reduce mediastinal TB.
sections.p: Monitor symptom resolution, treat underlying disease and avoid iatrogenic causes.

b: Angioedema – rapid facial swelling without venous collaterals.
Congestive heart failure – bilateral peripheral oedema, not isolated upper body.
Superior mediastinal syndrome from aortic aneurysm – pulsatile mass, not venous congestion.
sections.p: Conditions that cause upper‑body swelling but have different pathophysiology.

b: Chest X‑ray can be normal early; do not rule out obstruction if clinical signs are strong.
D‑dimer may be normal in chronic thrombosis; rely on imaging.
ESR elevation is non‑specific; it does not differentiate TB from lymphoma.
sections.p: Certain investigations may appear normal despite serious obstruction.
